title: Information-theoretic classical verification of quantum computation
formal:
Can a completely classical verifier check arbitrary efficient quantum computation by interacting with one efficient quantum prover, with soundness against every computationally unbounded cheating prover?

The common input is an explicitly encoded quantum circuit \(C\) over \(\{H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\}\), with all qubits initially zero and a designated output qubit. Write \(N\) for its description length and \(p(C)\) for the probability that measuring that output in the computational basis gives one. The promise is
\[C\in\mathrm{YES}\iff p(C)\ge 2/3,\qquad C\in\mathrm{NO}\iff p(C)\le 1/3.\]
Does there exist one uniform interactive protocol \((P,V)\) and positive integer constants \(a,d\) with the following properties? The verifier \(V\) is a classical probabilistic machine; the honest prover \(P\) is a quantum machine with classical control. They exchange only classical messages with no setup or extra prover. Both honest computations, the verifier against every cheating strategy, the number of messages and total communication have the polynomial bounds specified below. For every promised circuit,
\[C\in\mathrm{YES}\ \Longrightarrow\ \Pr[V\text{ accepts in interaction with }P\text{ on }C]\ge2/3,\]
\[C\in\mathrm{NO}\ \Longrightarrow\ \forall P^*\quad\Pr[V\text{ accepts in interaction with }P^*\text{ on }C]\le1/3.\]
Here \(P^*\) ranges over all adaptive response strategies, without any computational bound. The protocol and the constants precede the quantifiers over inputs and cheating strategies.
definitions:
A circuit consists of \(q\ge1\) labelled qubits, an ordered list \(g_1,\ldots,g_m\) of gates with \(m\ge0\), and an output index \(o\in\{1,\ldots,q\}\). The one-qubit matrices and two-qubit action are
\[H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mathrm{CNOT}|x,y\rangle=|x,x\mathbin\oplus y\rangle.\]
Here \(x,y\in\{0,1\}\) and \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. Each gate acts on its indicated qubit or ordered pair of distinct qubits and as the identity on the rest. Let \(U_C=g_m\cdots g_1\), with identity for an empty list. In the vector space \((\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes q}\), set
\[p(C)=\sum_{\substack{z\in\{0,1\}^q\\z_o=1}}|\langle z|U_C|0^q\rangle|^2.\]
These gate entries and probabilities are exact mathematical quantities, not floating-point input data. No correctness condition is imposed when \(1/3<p(C)<2/3\).

For a concrete bit encoding, write \(q\) as \(1^q0\), followed by \(U(m),U(o)\) and every gate in sequence. The length-delimited integer code is \(U(b)=1^\ell0s\), where \(s\) is the canonical binary expansion of \(b\ge0\), \(\ell=|s|\), and zero has expansion 0. A gate uses a two-bit tag for H, T or CNOT, followed by the \(U\)-encoded target indices; the fourth tag is invalid. All indices must be within the declared range and CNOT indices must be distinct. No trailing bits are allowed. Thus \(q\le N\) and all gates are explicitly listed. Both parties receive the same classical description; neither receives an additional quantum input or witness. Malformed descriptions are rejected by the verifier.

The two algorithms have fixed finite classical control programs, independent of \(N\) and \(C\). The verifier has ordinary classical work tapes, private independent fair random bits, and a classical message interface. It has no quantum register, quantum channel or ability to prepare, transform or measure qubits. The honest prover starts with zero qubits, may create zero ancillas, apply H, T and CNOT gates, measure qubits in the computational basis, and use outcomes in subsequent classical computation. Measurements follow the squared-amplitude rule; a measured qubit may be discarded. Its classical controller may also toss fair coins. Gate addresses, classical arithmetic and generation of the next instruction are computed and charged. There is no input-dependent or length-dependent advice, precomputed advice state or uncharged oracle for either honest party.

Put \(R(N)=a(N+1)^d\). On every input and every branch of its private randomness, the verifier uses at most \(R(N)\) classical bit steps, reads at most that many received bits, and halts with accept or reject. This clock holds against every possible sequence of replies. In an honest execution, the prover uses at most \(R(N)\) classical bit steps and elementary quantum operations in total, on every randomness and measurement branch. One elementary quantum operation acts on at most two addressed qubits; all classical bit operations and all written or read message bits are charged. The honest prover holds at most \(R(N)\) qubits. These bounds also apply to well-formed circuits outside the promise. The protocol allows at most \(R(N)\) messages and \(R(N)\) communicated bits in total; the verifier enforces the declared message lengths and aborts on a violation. A missing reply or an explicit abort is rejection. There is no constant-round requirement or uncharged preprocessing phase.

For soundness, an arbitrary prover strategy can be described by a conditional distribution on its next classical reply for each input and history of messages it has seen. It can have unlimited private memory and arbitrary input-dependent information, but cannot see the verifier's private coins except through sent messages. This description includes the observable behaviour of any quantum cheating prover through the classical interface; no bound on its computation, circuit size or internal state is assumed. Acceptance probabilities include all private randomness and measurement outcomes. There is no initial shared secret, correlated setup state, trusted third party, random oracle or enforced separation inside the single prover.

Completeness concerns the one fixed honest algorithm on all YES instances. Soundness concerns every strategy on each NO instance. The task is verification of this decision promise problem; it imposes no separate blindness, sampling-output or witness-preservation requirement. Fixed error constants are part of the specification, rather than a numerical approximation tolerance for the final answer.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence of such a protocol or its full logical negation. A positive answer must give uniform algorithms and universal polynomial resource bounds, prove completeness on every YES circuit, and prove the stated bound against all unbounded response strategies on every NO circuit. A negative answer must rule out every protocol in this model: for each resource-bounded pair, some YES input violates completeness or some NO input and cheating strategy violate soundness. A cryptographic argument sound only against efficient attackers, a quantum verifier, extra isolated provers, an inefficient honest prover or an impossibility theorem restricted to particular protocols does not settle this proposition.
why: The question isolates the resources needed for a classical user to trust a quantum answer. Known protocols obtain trust by giving the verifier some quantum capability, separating several devices, or assuming that particular computations are hard for an attacker. Resolving the stated conjunction would determine whether any of those additional resources is necessary when the honest server itself remains efficient.

importance.reason: A central quantum-complexity question connecting interactive proofs, delegation and the minimum resources needed to verify computations beyond classical simulation.

progress.text: The detailed classical-control manuscript uses separated entangled quantum subsystems.
The completed small-quantum-verifier treatment gives unbounded-cheater soundness and explicitly leaves removal of all verifier qubits open.
Classical single-prover verification is obtained under quantum LWE hardness, with computational soundness.
Witness-preserving classical QMA verification is claimed with negligible errors under post-quantum LWE.
A conditional black-box barrier is stated for one-message QMA verification; it does not rule out interactive BQP verification.
A relativizing classical multiprover containment is proved while efficient, unconditional single-prover verification is explicitly retained as open.
The trusted-gate verification article is published, retaining quantum client operations and communication.

status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The inspected April 2026 primary source explicitly leaves efficient, unconditional single-prover verification by a classical verifier open. Its relativizing MIP theorem does not supply one efficient honest prover. The February witness-preserving protocol retains LWE; the February non-interactive barrier concerns a restricted QMA model; and the May trusted-gate article retains quantum client operations. None meets or rules out the full conjunction specified here. No matching later resolution was found in the bounded search; individual cited proofs were not independently certified.

context_blocks.text: The honest-prover condition matters as much as the classical-verifier condition. The standard containments of quantum polynomial time in polynomial space, and IP=PSPACE, provide classical interactive proofs with an unrestricted prover. They do not establish that the auxiliary answers needed by that prover can be generated by a quantum polynomial-time machine. A verification protocol that demands a substantially more powerful server would not meet this card.

Aharonov, Ben-Or, Eban and Mahadev supply information-theoretically sound verification with an efficient quantum prover when the verifier retains a small quantum register. For a fixed error gap, a constant number of qubits suffices in their result. Although their class definition first restricts dishonest provers, they explicitly state that the protocol proof protects against unbounded provers. Eliminating the verifier’s remaining quantum capability is the open question highlighted in their §1.8.

Reichardt, Unger and Vazirani use separated entangled quantum subsystems. Their classical verifier can certify and control quantum operations under the noncommunication constraints of that model. A single freely communicating prover is allowed to coordinate its replies across all of its internal components, so combining the devices loses a condition used by the multiprover theorem.

Mahadev’s protocol achieves the classical verifier and single efficient quantum prover by using a computational assumption. The inspected version bases its construction on quantum hardness of Learning With Errors with the specified superpolynomial noise ratio. Its soundness quantifies over efficient quantum cheating algorithms. An unbounded strategy is outside that guarantee, even if the protocol is otherwise fully classical at the interface.

The February 2026 quantum-cat preprint addresses preservation of a quantum witness: the prover can reuse one copy while obtaining negligible errors. Its abstract retains the post-quantum LWE assumption. A QMA witness is an additional quantum input that is not present in the all-zero BQP computation here, and preserving it does not remove the computational soundness assumption.

Another February 2026 preprint gives a conditional barrier to quantum black-box reductions for non-interactive QMA verification from falsifiable assumptions. Its model has one message after instance-independent setup, and its premise is a QMA–QCMA gap problem. Both the task and the restrictions differ from this card’s arbitrary polynomial interaction for BQP. The checked abstract therefore supplies no general impossibility answer here.

The April 2026 paper proves \(\mathrm{BQP}^{O}\subseteq\mathrm{MIP}^{O}\) for every classical oracle \(O\). Its associated classical proof is exponentially long but checked at polynomially many adaptively chosen locations. The theorem concerns several classical provers without shared entanglement, and it does not promise that their honest work is quantum polynomial time. Section 2 separately asks for such an efficient-prover result. The paper presents relativization as a research perspective, not as an equivalence resolving single-prover verification.

The May 2026 trusted-gate article removes trusted state preparation and measurement from the client’s requirements while retaining trusted quantum transformations. Its first construction uses single-qubit rotations and bit flips; the inspected preprint explicitly sends qubits through the client. Removing two hardware capabilities is useful progress, but the client still has quantum operations and quantum communication. It is not the classical machine specified here.

For this question, “information-theoretic” is a quantifier about every cheating strategy. It does not require perfect completeness, zero soundness error, blindness or verification of an entire output distribution. Keeping these notions distinct prevents either a stronger unrelated task or a weaker computational guarantee from replacing the stated decision problem.

sentences: A classical user wants to check whether an explicitly given quantum circuit accepts with high probability.
One uniform quantum polynomial-time honest prover must convince the user on every YES circuit using only classical messages.
The verifier must reject NO circuits with high probability even against an unbounded adaptive cheating strategy.
Known positive results use limited quantum verifier resources, separated provers, or computational hardness assumptions.
The inspected 2026 literature retains the full single-prover information-theoretic question as open; narrower new protocols and barriers do not settle it.
